Abstract: Efficient irrigation allocation is essential for sustaining grain production while limiting water consumption in the North China Plain wheat–maize rotation. How spatial targeting redistributes production losses, and whether regional water-storage information improves rainfall-based irrigation decisions, remain unresolved. Continuous process-based crop simulations compared uniform and targeted allocations under equal irrigation budgets and evaluated annual storage–rainfall strategies against matched rainfall-only controls during 2014–2025. Growth parameters were fitted to multisite observations; water-use parameters were calibrated against Wuqiao treatments in 2016–2018 and retrospectively tested in 2019. At a 50% irrigation reduction, targeting retained 0.73 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ more simulated combined dry grain than uniform cuts across 9.87 million rotation hectares, equivalent to 7.22 million t yr⁻¹ or 4.87% of uniform production. Mean production was lower than under uniform cuts on 37.60% of mapped area, while crop-plus-fallow evapotranspiration increased by 20.76 mm yr⁻¹ (2.05 km³ yr⁻¹). Across nine years with eligible Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) observations, strategies selected at 95% and 98% grain targets retained 96.27% and 99.63% of conventional production, respectively. The 95% strategy reduced irrigation by 130.72 mm and evapotranspiration by 36.84 mm per rotation. Matched storage–rainfall and rainfall-only strategies selected identical quotas and produced identical outcomes. These conditional results support joint production and consumptive-use constraints and local production safeguards, while showing that additional storage information provides no decision benefit within the tested quota design.
1. Introduction: Irrigation management in the North China Plain must reconcile grain production with water-resource constraints across the winter wheat–summer maize rotation [CITE:yang2022_long_term_irrigation]. Wheat grows through a relatively dry season, whereas maize receives more summer rainfall; soil-water reserves connect their responses to irrigation [CITE:yang2024_precipitation]. Long-term well-watered observations show that rising grain yield has accompanied increasing actual evapotranspiration (ET), despite comparatively stable reference ET [CITE:zhang2011_et_change]. Maintaining production with less irrigation therefore requires attention to both the water delivered to fields and the water consumed over the complete rotation.

The timing and location of irrigation supply determine its marginal production return. A sixteen-year experiment in 2003–2018 compared seven wheat–maize irrigation schedules and found diminishing production gains as irrigation increased [CITE:yang2022_long_term_irrigation]. A four-year Wuqiao experiment also showed that precipitation conditions influenced the preferred wheat schedule and grain production in the subsequent maize crop [CITE:yang2024_precipitation]. These responses reflect the sequence of crop demand, rainfall and soil-water carry-over across both seasons [CITE:yang2022_long_term_irrigation|yang2024_precipitation]. At regional scale, irrigation requirements vary among locations and hydrological years [CITE:wu2019_spatial_irrigation|ren2022_regional_water]. Crop-model optimization and irrigation-allocation studies provide approaches for using this heterogeneity to guide management [CITE:xiao2024_management_optimization|jiang2016_regional_optimization]. Under a common water budget, targeting locations with larger marginal grain returns can improve regional production retention, while changing the distribution of production losses.

Assessing these allocation consequences requires consistent crop and water accounting. Field delivery, ET, return flows and storage changes describe different quantities, so a reduction in irrigation does not directly establish an equivalent reduction in consumption [CITE:perry2009_water_accounting|grafton2018_irrigation_paradox]. Process-based applications of APSIM and RZ-SHAW in the North China Plain connect crop production with water productivity, field water balance and ET [CITE:chen2010_climate_water|fang2014]. However, transpiration formulation remains a major source of variation in simulated wheat water use [CITE:cammarano2016_water_use]. Phenology, canopy, biomass, grain and ET observations therefore constrain complementary processes, while documented irrigation treatments assess their combined response to water supply. Continuous simulation retains the soil-water carry-over needed to compare complete rotation histories.

Spatial allocation determines where irrigation is supplied, while antecedent hydrological conditions can inform the annual irrigation budget. Recent rainfall describes water input at the crop-system scale, whereas GRACE total water storage integrates several terrestrial stores over a regional footprint [CITE:save2016_csr_mascons|scanlon2016_grace_mascons]. Recent aquifer recovery under water transfers, abstraction management and changing climate illustrates the broader context of regional storage variation [CITE:long2025_aquifer_recovery|xu2026_groundwater_recovery]. Storage information may thus characterize conditions beyond local rainfall. Its practical value for irrigation nevertheless depends on whether it changes the selected action or improves the resulting grain–water outcome relative to rainfall-based decisions.

Two connected management questions remain unresolved. First, it is unclear how much grain spatial targeting can retain under an identical irrigation budget, and what consumptive-water costs and persistent local production losses accompany that regional benefit. Rotation-wide accounting must retain soil-water carry-over to assess these outcomes together. Second, the additional decision value of regional storage information beyond antecedent rainfall remains uncertain. A storage indicator can distinguish hydrological conditions without changing an irrigation choice. Comparisons using the same production targets, candidate quotas and monitoring availability are needed to isolate its contribution to management outcomes.

The objectives were to (i) quantify rotation grain production, crop-plus-fallow ET and profile drainage under uniform and spatially targeted irrigation allocations with common regional water budgets; (ii) characterize the spatial distribution, magnitude and annual persistence of allocation-related grain gains and losses; and (iii) assess whether antecedent regional storage information changes annual irrigation quotas and grain–water outcomes relative to rainfall-only controls under matched selection and monitoring conditions. Continuous Open Crop Model simulations of the North China Plain wheat–maize rotation, parameterized using multisite crop observations and documented irrigation treatments, provide the basis for these conditional comparisons during 2014–2025.
2.1. Overall workflow: The framework connects crop-response estimation with spatial allocation and annual irrigation-quota selection (Figure 1). Multisite crop observations support growth-parameter estimates, while documented Wuqiao treatments in 2016–2018 constrain eight water coefficients per crop. Wuqiao 2019 provides retrospective testing; station observations characterize transfer under the recorded management and initialization. Observation coverage and the distinct estimation and evaluation partitions are summarized in Figure 3. Daily weather, mapped rotation area and layered soil profiles define 32 regional representatives.

The same crop and water parameters drive continuous crop and fallow histories under five irrigation levels. Spatial allocations selected from 1997–2013 responses share identical regional delivery budgets with uniform reductions. Annual storage–rainfall and rainfall-only strategies are selected from matched 2003–2013 responses and compared with common monitoring availability. Grain production, field irrigation, crop-plus-fallow ET and profile drainage are evaluated during 2014–2025.
2.11. Continuous class-adaptive irrigati: Two annual strategies apply the irrigation fractions selected from fixed-fraction responses at grain-retention targets of 95% and 98%. At each simulation unit, the antecedent storage–rainfall class determines the fraction before wheat sowing. This fraction scales all four wheat applications and the subsequent maize application in the same rotation year. Application dates, crop parameters, weather, hydraulic profiles and the free-drainage lower boundary are identical to those in the fixed-fraction experiment. Conventional irrigation applies before 2003 and whenever an eligible storage class is unavailable, including evaluation harvest years 2014, 2018 and 2019.

Each strategy is simulated continuously from the 1996 spin-up through 2025. Soil-water states pass between crops and fallows and across annual changes in irrigation fraction. Conventional irrigation supplies the paired continuous reference; replays at two simulation units verify the scenario driver against conventional outputs. Class thresholds and irrigation fractions remain fixed after selection. Outcomes cover all twelve comparison years and, separately, the nine years with eligible classes. Production retention is the ratio of period-mean regional grain production to its corresponding conventional mean; annual ratios describe variation within the period. The strategies assume access to antecedent observation periods, while release availability of GRACE before sowing remains unverified.
3.3. Grain production and water balance: Conventional irrigation supplied 37.493 km³ yr⁻¹ and produced 165.321 million t yr⁻¹ of simulated dry grain during 2014–2025. At a 50% irrigation cut, uniform and targeted allocation each supplied 18.747 km³ yr⁻¹. Targeted production was 155.509 million t yr⁻¹, compared with 148.290 million t yr⁻¹ under uniform cuts. Targeting therefore retained 0.732 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ more dry grain across the fixed 9,866,602-ha rotation area. The corresponding reduction in regional grain loss was 7.219 million t yr⁻¹, or 4.87% of uniform production (Table 4). Targeted production remained 9.813 million t yr⁻¹ below conventional production. Annual grain totals combine wheat and maize harvests from the same rotation hectares.

Crop-plus-fallow ET was 81.666 km³ yr⁻¹ under targeting and 79.617 km³ yr⁻¹ under uniform allocation, compared with 87.559 km³ yr⁻¹ under conventional irrigation. Targeting therefore increased ET by 2.048 km³ yr⁻¹ under the same delivery constraint. Profile drainage was 7.799 versus 9.506 km³ yr⁻¹, and runoff was 1.424 versus 1.874 km³ yr⁻¹ (Table 4; Figure 6).

The targeted-minus-uniform regional grain contrast was positive in all twelve years. Central and northern latitude bands contributed gains of 7.475 and 1.886 million t yr⁻¹, while the southern band contributed a loss of 2.142 million t yr⁻¹. The southern band occupied 60.7% of mapped rotation area. Corresponding band-mean rotation-yield changes were +2.415, +2.420 and −0.357 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in the central, northern and southern bands, respectively (Figure 7; Table S9).
4. Discussion: The simulations reveal three linked dimensions of irrigation management: production retained under a delivery constraint, consumptive water use and the distribution of production changes. Spatial targeting improves regional grain production by assigning a fixed budget to more responsive crop–soil–climate systems. Annual rainfall–storage strategies instead change the delivered quota in response to antecedent conditions. Both decisions operate through crop stress and the soil water carried between wheat, maize and fallow periods. Their management value consequently depends on the complete rotation response, the accounting boundary used to define a water saving and the reliability of the crop responses underlying selection.
4.1. Marginal irrigation returns and spa: Spatial targeting exploits differences in marginal grain response to irrigation. Diminishing production gains across field schedules [CITE:yang2022_long_term_irrigation] and spatial variation in irrigation requirements [CITE:wu2019_spatial_irrigation] provide a basis for redistributing a limited supply, consistent with regional allocation studies [CITE:jiang2016_regional_optimization]. The equal-budget comparison attributes the simulated production difference to delivery allocation. Complete continuous histories retain the effects of earlier irrigation and rainfall on subsequent crop responses.

At the 50% delivery reduction, targeting retained 0.732 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ more combined wheat–maize dry grain than uniform cuts. Across 9.8666 million rotation hectares, the corresponding reduction in grain loss was 7.219 million t yr⁻¹, or 4.87% of the uniform total. Targeted production remained below conventional production. The positive contrast in all twelve years indicates consistent regional gains within the simulated record. Its magnitude remains dependent on the crop-response functions and declared management schedules (Table 4; Figure 6).

Regional gain has a pronounced distributional cost. Central and northern band-mean rotation yields increased by 2.415 and 2.420 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, while the southern mean decreased by 0.357 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. The southern band covers 60.7% of the rotation area, so its losses substantially offset gains elsewhere (Figure 7; Table S9). The production objective maximizes the area-weighted regional total and supplies no minimum yield for an individual location. Local production floors and constraints on the distribution of irrigation reductions are therefore separate requirements for allocation that protects affected farms.
4.2. Rotation carry-over and the timing: The spatial production response integrates water effects across both crops. Wheat irrigation can support canopy growth and grain formation, replenish water available to maize or increase drainage. Reduced wheat delivery can increase subsequent dependence on summer rainfall, producing different annual grain responses under different rainfall sequences. The sixteen-year irrigation experiment shows diminishing production gains, and the Wuqiao experiment links precipitation conditions with wheat scheduling and subsequent maize production [CITE:yang2022_long_term_irrigation|yang2024_precipitation]. These coupled responses make the complete rotation the relevant unit for irrigation allocation.

Continuous soil-water histories preserve the delayed benefits and costs of allocation and annual quota changes (Figure S3). Production can be maintained by drawing down profile storage, with later rainfall or irrigation determining its replenishment. A finite-period delivery reduction can therefore include a contribution from stored soil water. Crop-plus-fallow accounting also captures evaporation and drainage between harvest and sowing. Their inclusion connects apparent production retention with the water remaining for the next crop and the complete rotation water balance.

The field evidence constrains only part of this carry-over mechanism. Wuqiao simulations use reported total profile storage with an assumed layer distribution. Wheat crop-start storage follows the pre-sowing simulation, whereas maize is independently initialized from treatment-specific observations. Maize irrigation is identical among treatments within each year, and its treatment labels identify preceding wheat schedules [CITE:yang2024_precipitation]. Maize comparisons thus evaluate crop responses to the initial state associated with wheat management (Figure 5; Figure S2). Regional carry-over additionally depends on the model's continuous propagation and vertical redistribution of water between crops.
4.3. Production, consumptive use and gro: The production benefit of targeting carries a consumptive-use trade-off. At the common 50% delivery reduction, targeting increased ET by 2.048 km³ yr⁻¹ and reduced profile drainage by 1.707 km³ yr⁻¹ relative to uniform allocation. With rainfall and total irrigation held constant, differences in ET are balanced by drainage, runoff and soil-storage change (Table 4). A shared delivery constraint therefore permits different consumptive outcomes. Irrigation productivity and consumptive-water savings require distinct objectives [CITE:perry2009_water_accounting|grafton2018_irrigation_paradox].

The soil-profile balance also has a different boundary from the aquifer balance. Drainage below 2 m enters a deeper vadose zone, with storage and transit outside the modeled profile [CITE:wu2023_vadose_zone]. Reduced field delivery or profile drainage therefore provides insufficient information to quantify changes in pumping, aquifer recharge or groundwater storage. Production and ET comparisons can identify agronomic trade-offs, while groundwater outcomes require the corresponding subsurface and abstraction accounting.

GRACE offers regional storage context at a broader scale. Its anomalies integrate groundwater with other terrestrial stores, and its effective observation scale exceeds the displayed grid resolution [CITE:save2016_csr_mascons|scanlon2016_grace_mascons]. Recent aquifer recovery reflects water transfers, abstraction management and hydroclimatic conditions [CITE:long2025_aquifer_recovery|xu2026_groundwater_recovery]. The crop-model scenarios quantify changes in field delivery, consumption and profile outflow without attributing those observed storage changes to individual irrigation strategies.
4.4. When storage information changes an: A storage indicator adds decision value when its inclusion changes the selected action or improves the grain–water outcome under common constraints. GRACE represents regional storage conditions, while antecedent rainfall describes more local water input [CITE:save2016_csr_mascons|scanlon2016_grace_mascons]. Their different physical support motivates joint classification, but decision value also depends on how the resulting classes distinguish among the available irrigation fractions.

Both storage strata selected the same fraction for a given rainfall group at the 95% and 98% grain targets. Storage–rainfall and matched rainfall-only strategies consequently produced identical complete histories of irrigation, crop states, grain, ET and drainage. The storage split supplied additional environmental description without changing an irrigation action in this five-level quota design. All nine later years with eligible observations fell in the lower-storage category, so the higher-storage choices also lacked later-period exposure (Table 5; Figure 8). These features delimit the configuration and conditions represented by the equal outcomes.

Monitoring coverage must remain distinct from the grouping criterion. Rainfall-available controls can change irrigation during GRACE gaps, and those earlier decisions alter the soil-water state inherited in later years. Their outcomes therefore combine rainfall-based selection with additional years of management. Matched coverage preserves the appropriate comparison for the incremental effect of storage information. Finer quota choices, alternative thresholds and verified release availability would define different decision experiments with their own selection and evaluation requirements.
4.5. Crop-response constraints and manag: Management selection depends on the modeled marginal response to water, in addition to absolute grain and canopy agreement. Intercepted-PAR radiation-use efficiency [CITE:kiniry1989_rue], cohort-specific leaf area and thermal senescence connect canopy development with carbon supply; grain number and fixed individual grain mass constrain the sink. Root uptake and the assimilation stress exponent then determine how water shortage changes production. Variation among wheat-model transpiration formulations demonstrates the sensitivity of water-use predictions to these processes [CITE:cammarano2016_water_use]. Water coefficients near their prescribed bounds remain effective empirical estimates whose physiological interpretation and uniqueness are limited.

The estimation and evaluation data provide different evidence for these responses. Earlier growth estimates use 480 wheat and 433 maize observations across four wheat sites and five maize sites, with whole site-years and balanced site contributions. Incomplete station irrigation histories limit transfer comparisons, and station observations have no weight in the fitted water-response objective. Wuqiao 2016–2018 supplies the documented treatment seasons for that fit. Wuqiao 2019 supplies a single test year with reported total storage, assumed layer distributions and transferred soil hydraulics; prior inspection of its outcomes makes the test retrospective (Figures 3–5). Regional comparison years also overlap crop-fitting years, so regional production differences characterize model scenarios rather than time-forward crop validation.

Substantial field-test errors constrain confidence in irrigation-response transfer. Wheat grain nRMSE was 83.27%, with a bias of +3.108 t ha⁻¹ at the published 13% moisture basis; the absolute W3−W0 ET-contrast error was 116.37 mm. Maize ET NSE was negative, with an ET-contrast error of 52.74 mm (Table 3; Table S5). These discrepancies affect the response functions used to select regional allocations. Numerical water-balance closure demonstrates conservation but supplies no measure of response accuracy. The eight purposive actual-cell checks address a separate uncertainty, spatial aggregation, and provide no regional field-validation sample. Depth-resolved soil water and complete dated management would better constrain uptake and redistribution; canopy and soil-moisture assimilation also requires treatment of retrieval errors and observation operators [CITE:ines2013_soil_lai_assimilation].

Production-retention targets introduce a further management distinction between period means and annual reliability. Mean retention of 96.27% and 99.63% coincided with annual minima of 92.12% and 98.58%; the 95% strategy met that threshold in eight of nine class-available years (Figure 8). A mean target consequently supplies no shortfall probability or guarantee for an individual farm. Local production floors, acceptable shortfall frequency and a reserve entering the next crop can complement regional delivery and consumption constraints. Forecast-based irrigation studies illustrate explicit treatment of water-stress risk [CITE:roy2021_irrigation_risk]. Field scheduling additionally requires current soil-water information, weather forecasts and application timing.
5. Conclusions: At an identical 50% reduction in field irrigation, targeted allocation retained 0.732 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ more simulated wheat–maize dry grain than uniform cuts during 2014–2025. This reduced regional grain loss by 7.219 million t yr⁻¹, equivalent to 4.87% of uniform production. It coincided with 2.048 km³ yr⁻¹ greater crop-plus-fallow ET. Central and northern gains outweighed southern losses, demonstrating that regional production retention, consumptive use and local production outcomes require separate management constraints.

Annual strategies selected at 95% and 98% grain-retention targets retained 96.27% and 99.63% of conventional production over nine years with eligible GRACE observations. The 95% strategy reduced irrigation by 130.72 mm and ET by 36.84 mm per rotation. Matched rainfall-only controls selected identical quotas and produced identical outcomes, so storage classification provided no additional decision benefit within the tested quota design and monitoring coverage.

Continuous rotation accounting preserves the influence of preceding management on subsequent production and water use. The field-test errors and incomplete station management delimit confidence in transferring the estimated crop responses. Translation of these regional scenarios into irrigation management depends on observed response accuracy, explicit production-risk constraints and field scheduling informed by soil water and forecasts. Groundwater effects additionally require pumping, recharge and deeper subsurface storage beyond the crop-model boundary.
2.12. Rainfall-only controls and storage: Rainfall-only controls use the same 2003–2013 simulation-unit years with eligible GRACE observations, the same rotation-area weights, irrigation candidates and grain-retention targets. Selection groups responses by antecedent rainfall alone and chooses the lowest fraction meeting the relevant target. The rainfall threshold is identical to that in the joint classification. Matched controls receive conventional irrigation whenever the storage–rainfall strategy lacks an eligible class, preserving both the selection cohort and monitoring coverage. Continuous differences between these paired strategies consequently assess the incremental effect of storage-based grouping.

Separate rainfall-available controls apply the selected rainfall-only fractions whenever an eligible rainfall group exists, including years without GRACE coverage. Their complete histories assess the combined effect of rainfall-based management and greater monitoring availability. Irrigation changes in earlier gap years can alter the soil-water state of later crops, so these controls are reported separately from the matched comparison.
4.6. Limitations and future directions: The principal limitation is uncertainty in the crop responses used for strategy selection. Field testing covers a single, previously inspected year, while incomplete station management and assumed initial water profiles constrain transfer. Remaining errors in ET and grain responses prevent the simulated policy advantages from being interpreted as independently validated field benefits. Further evaluation requires new site-years with complete management records, withheld from both model development and strategy selection. Concurrent measurements of soil water by depth, ET, canopy development and harvest would allow separate assessment of water redistribution, crop stress and irrigation-treatment contrasts.

Regional results also depend on a static rotation map, representative climate–soil units, prescribed irrigation dates and fixed nutrition modifiers. Checks at purposively selected source cells cannot bound regional uncertainty. Dynamic nitrogen cycling is absent, and changes in crop area or actual farm practices are not reconstructed. Future analyses should expand evaluation at individual source cells and propagate uncertainty in crop parameters, soil hydraulics, weather and spatial aggregation through paired policy histories. Allocation stability and the magnitude and persistence of local losses require uncertainty assessment alongside the regional mean.

The storage comparison is specific to the tested quota grid, classification thresholds and lower-storage conditions represented during later comparison years. GRACE release availability before sowing remains unverified, so the scenarios do not establish operational scheduling performance. Prospective decision experiments should use information available on each decision date, maintain matched rainfall-only controls and evaluate both storage states. Finer quotas and application timing informed by soil water could be tested with constraints on consumptive use, local production and the risk of production shortfalls.

Finally, the profile uses free drainage at its lower boundary, with no capillary supply or deeper subsurface storage, and field irrigation is not linked to measured abstraction. Groundwater applications require joint accounting of soil water and aquifer flows, constrained by observations of pumping, recharge and storage change. Delivery capacity, irrigation costs and farmer participation also require assessment before the agronomic scenarios can support operational management.
2.3.3. Meteorological, soil, crop-rotati: Daily AgERA5 v2.0 weather data on the common 0.1° grid supplied minimum and maximum air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, reference evapotranspiration, vapor pressure and 10-m wind speed for 1996–2025 [CITE:agera5]. Reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) entered the water-balance module directly.

Native 250 m SoilGrids v2.0 maps of texture, bulk density, organic carbon and coarse fragments were averaged to 0.01°, then aggregated over mapped rotation pixels within 0.1° meteorological cells, for six depth intervals between 0 and 2 m [CITE:soilgrids2020_dataset]. Hydraulic properties were derived using Saxton–Rawls equations with bulk-density and gravel adjustments [CITE:saxton2006_hydraulics]. Organic matter was approximated using an assumed organic-matter/organic-carbon ratio of 1.724, and air-dry water content was assumed to equal half the wilting-point value. Hydraulic derivation is detailed in Supplementary Section S2.

The 500 m ChinaCP map for 2020 identified winter-wheat–summer-maize rotation pixels, which were paired with the corresponding CPM cropland-percentage map [CITE:chinacp2022]. Physical classified-cell areas were corrected for projection scale and multiplied by cropland percentages to obtain rotation-area weights. CPM values were sampled at ChinaCP pixel centers after coordinate transformation because the source grids had different origins. Pixel centers assigned these weights to the study domain and 0.1° meteorological cells. The fixed 2020 footprint supplied a common area basis across climate years; the area and mapping sensitivity analyses are described in Section 2.2 and Supplementary Section S3.

SRTMGL1 v003 elevation was bilinearly resampled to 0.001°, and slope was derived at that support [CITE:srtm]. Aligned 10 × 10 cell means provided elevation and slope on the 0.01° grid used for lowland screening in Section 2.2. Crop-area weights and aggregated soil profiles were linked to daily weather through common 0.1° cell identifiers.

review_findings.issue: The regional grain-production difference can be mistaken for a per-hectare yield difference, while its comparator and annual wheat–maize basis are insufficiently prominent.
review_findings.resolution: State the targeted-minus-uniform 7.219 million t yr⁻¹ contrast together with its fixed-area mean, 0.732 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, its 4.87% uniform-production denominator and its combined annual wheat–maize dry-grain basis.

review_findings.issue: The production–consumption distinction and the relationship between spatial allocation and annual quota selection become clear only late in the introduction.
review_findings.resolution: Use a six-paragraph progression from regional production and water objectives through rotation dependence, spatial allocation, crop-response evidence and hydrological information to the two management comparisons.

review_findings.issue: GRACE data follow evaluation metrics, and spatial allocation, class construction and continuous annual strategies are split into separate top-level methods sections.
review_findings.resolution: Move GRACE observations to 2.3.4; group spatial allocation, annual quota selection and continuous comparisons in 2.7 Irrigation strategies; retain metrics and water accounting as the final Methods section.

review_findings.issue: Quota selection, continuous annual strategies and matched controls appear in separate top-level sections, making their shared selection and comparison framework harder to follow.
review_findings.resolution: Combine the existing selection and strategy definitions under annual irrigation quotas and the existing rainfall-only definitions under matched controls; retain their common selection cohort, weighting, rainfall threshold, fallback and distinct monitoring-availability sensitivity.

review_findings.issue: The evidence-partition figure performs a Methods role even though its discussion is presented at the start of Results.
review_findings.resolution: Place Figure 3 with observation coverage and estimation/evaluation definitions, refer to it in 2.1, and begin Results with crop-performance findings.

review_findings.issue: Repeated numerical summaries and provenance qualifiers interrupt the sequence from production benefit to distribution, carry-over, water accounting, information value and reliability.
review_findings.resolution: Give each subsection one distinct inferential role and concentrate evidence limitations in 4.5, while retaining essential field-initialization boundaries in 4.2 and water-accounting boundaries in 4.3.

unit_binding.grain_basis: Simulated dry grain; annual sum of wheat and maize harvests over the same rotation hectares.
unit_binding.comparison: Targeted minus uniform allocation; both deliver the identical 50%-reduced regional field-irrigation volume.
unit_binding.effect_interpretation: Less grain loss than uniform allocation at the same irrigation cut; targeted production remains below conventional production.
